game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 7, 9, 11, 11, 12.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 4, 11.
- Die 3 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 4, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 15.9: die 1 averages 8.67, die 2 averages 4.75 and die 3 averages 2.5. The standard deviation of the sum is about 5.7. The share of informed traders could be high (alpha is 0.48 on average), so I quote a wide spread centred on 15.9.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 19.9}

Die 2 came up 1, so the fair value is about 12.2:

- **Die 1** averages 52/6 ≈ 8.67.
- **Die 2** is 1.
- **Die 3** averages 10/4 = 2.5.

**Earlier trades:** with die 2 = 1, the most the contract can settle at is 12 + 1 + 6 = 19. Both buyers paid more than that (19.9 and 21.5). An informed trader would only have paid that much if die 2 were 11. So these two trades say nothing about die 1 or die 3, and they are mildly consistent with a lower alpha.

**Quote:** I am short 2 at an average price of about 20.7, so I'm comfortably in profit. I'll skew my quotes upward around fair value to make it more likely I buy back.

{"bid": 11.8, "ask": 14.6}

Die 2 = 1, so the settlement value is 1 plus die 1 plus die 3. With no other information, die 1 averages about 8.67 and die 3 averages 2.5, giving a fair value of about 12.2.

The buy at 14.6 after the reveal points to a high value. If that buyer was informed, die 1 plus die 3 is at least 14, so settlement is at least 15. That shifts my estimate upward, to about 14.

I am short 3, so buying back a unit lowers my risk. An informed counterparty would only sell to me if settlement is below my bid, and a bid of 13 makes that unlikely given the evidence. A noise trader whose valuation falls below 13 would sell to me, which is a good fill.

Round 1: buyers at 19.9 and 21.5 when settlement was 13, so those were likely noise traders, which points to lower alpha. No trade at 13/18.9 is consistent with noise, since the probability of no trade is moderate.

I'll quote around 15.9 with a fairly wide spread.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 18.6}

Expected settlement is about 14.2 before adjusting for trade flow.
- Die 1 averages 52/6 ≈ 8.67, die 3 averages 2.5, and die 2 is revealed as 3.

**Evidence on alpha (how many counterparties are informed):**
- In round 1, counterparties bought at 19.9 and 21.5, then the contract settled at 13.
- Informed traders would not have bought that high, so those were noise traders.
- That points to alpha being low.

**Evidence from this round:**
- Someone sold to me at 13.4. That hints mildly that the value is low, for example die 1 = 2, or die 1 + die 3 ≤ 10.
- Since alpha is probably low, I nudge fair value only slightly down, to about 13.9.

**Quote:**
- I'm long 1 unit, so I skew the quote slightly down to encourage a sale over another buy.
- The spread stays wide to protect against informed traders.

In round 1 the counterparties bought at 19.9 and 21.5 when the contract settled at 13. That points to noise traders, so alpha may well be low. Even so, the seller at 13.4 in this round could have been informed.

I'm long one unit, so I lean the quotes slightly downward. That makes a sale, which would flatten my position, a bit more likely.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 16.2}

The expected value comes from adding the mean of each die:

Die 1 mean = (2+7+9+11+11+12)/6 = 52/6 ≈ 8.67. Die 3 mean = 2.5. With die 2 = 3, expected value ≈ 14.17.

Possible sums are die1 + 3 + die3. With die1 ∈ {2, 7, 9, 11, 11, 12} and die3 ∈ {0, 0, 4, 6}, the sums are spread from 5 to 21.

I'll quote a bid of 11.0 and an ask of 15.8, with a slight skew to reduce the long position.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 2, 4 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 6, 4 cards worth 7, 4 cards worth 11, 4 cards worth 15. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before any card is shown, the expected sum of the two cards is about 13.8, with a standard deviation of about 7.2. I don't know how many counterparties are informed, so I'm quoting a wide spread around 13.8.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 18.7}

A seller hit my bid at 9, which is weak evidence the sum is low.

**Prior fair value.** The deck's 22 cards total 152, so the average card is about 6.91. The expected sum of two cards is about 13.8.

**Reading the trade.**
- A noise trader would sell below 9 only about 22% of the time, because 9 is about 0.78 standard deviations below the 13.8 mean.
- An informed trader sells only when the true sum is below 9. I estimate that happens roughly a third of the time.
- So the sale is more likely when the sum is low, and I shade my estimate down to about 12.5.

**Quote.** I'm already long one unit, so I keep the bid low and set the ask a little tighter than last time to make selling easier.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 17}

Card 1 is a 3, so 21 cards remain, worth 149 in total. Card 2 averages about 7.1, which puts the public expected sum near 10.1.

The trade history pulls that down. On quote 1 a counterparty sold to me at 9. That is more likely if card 2 is low, because an informed seller would only sell below their known value. On quote 2 nobody traded at 8/17. That partly offsets the first signal, since an informed trader holding a low value would probably have sold at 8.

I put the fair value at roughly 8–9. I'm already long 1, so I set a fairly wide quote that leans slightly low.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 11.5}

No trade at 8.5/19.5, and that gives little information. The unconditional expected sum of two cards is about 13.8. Round 1's one-sided selling suggests a meaningful share of informed traders, so I'll keep the spread wide around 13.8.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 18.6}

Card 1 is 0, so the contract settles at the value of card 2.

**Prior on card 2.** The 21 cards left in the deck sum to 152, so the unconditional mean is about 7.2.

**Update from the stage-1 sell at 9.** That sell is evidence that card 2 is below 9, meaning it is one of 0, 2, 3, 6 or 7.
- Round 1 had three sells and settled at 3. That suggests alpha is high, so I assume about 0.6.
- Under that assumption, a sell at 9 is likely about 84% of the time when card 2 is low and about 24% when it is high (11 or 15).
- Weighting the remaining cards by these likelihoods gives a posterior mean of about 5.1.

**Quote.** I centre around 5 with a fairly wide spread, because informed traders may be common. I am already long 1, so I set the bid a little lower.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 7.5}

Card 1 is 0, so the contract settles at card 2's value. The two trades this round point in opposite directions:

- **Stage 1 sell at 9:** if the seller was informed, the sum was below 9, so card 2 is one of 0, 2, 3, 6 or 7.
- **Stage 2 buy at 7.5:** if the buyer was informed, card 2 is above 7.5, so it is 11 or 15.

At least one of these was a noise trader, so I can't lean hard either way. With no other information, card 2's expected value from the remaining 21 cards is about 7.2. Round 1's trades fit a fairly high share of informed traders, so I'm keeping the spread wide.

I'm quoting around a centre of 7.5–8, with a bid of 4 and an ask of 12. A sale at 4 only happens if card 2 is 0, 2 or 3. A buy at 12 only happens if card 2 is 15.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 5, 5, 8, 9, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 6, 10.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 4, 9, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 9.4. I'm quoting roughly 1 point either side of it because I don't yet know what share of counterparties are informed.

**Expected value of the max**

1. If die 3 shows 12 (probability 1/3), the max is 12.
2. Otherwise, take M = max(die 1, die 2), found from the product of their cumulative distributions:
   - P(M ≤ 3) = 1/12
   - P(M ≤ 5) = 1/4
   - P(M ≤ 7) = 3/8
   - P(M ≤ 8) = 1/2
   - P(M ≤ 9) = 5/8
   - P(M ≤ 10) = 1
   - This gives E[M] ≈ 7.71.
3. Combining M with each remaining face of die 3:
   - Die 3 = 1 or 3: the expected max is 7.71, since M is never below 3.
   - Die 3 = 4: it is 7.79, because a 4 beats M = 3.
   - Die 3 = 9: it is 9.375.
4. Overall: (1/6)(7.71 + 7.71 + 7.79 + 9.375) + (1/3)(12) ≈ 9.43.

**Quote**

The share of informed counterparties could be as high as 0.9, so I'm setting a fairly wide spread around 9.4.

game.description: A custom deck of 11 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 4 cards worth 1, 1 card worth 2, 1 card worth 6, 2 cards worth 8, 1 card worth 12. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The contract settles at the largest of the 3 cards dealt from the 11-card deck. Before any reveal, its expected value is about 7.44.

**Distribution of the maximum.** There are C(11,3) = 165 equally likely hands.

| Max card | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | 45 | 0.273 |
| 8 | 64 | 0.388 |
| 6 | 21 | 0.127 |
| 2 | 15 | 0.091 |
| 1 | 20 | 0.121 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |

The expected value is 1228 / 165 ≈ 7.44.

**Spread.** The settlement value is spread widely, from 1 up to 12. I don't yet know what share of counterparties are informed, and it could be as high as 0.9. So I quote a wide spread centred near 7.4 to limit losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 5.4, "ask": 9.6}

The first counterparty bought at my ask of 9.6, which is strong evidence that the max card is 12. That is the only possible value above 9.6, so I'm raising my fair value from 7.4 to about 10.0.

**Prior value before any trades**
- The deck has 11 cards, so there are C(11,3) = 165 possible hands. I counted how many hands have each possible largest card:

| Largest card | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | 45 | 0.273 |
| 8 | 64 | 0.388 |
| 6 | 21 | 0.127 |
| 2 | 15 | 0.091 |
| 1 | 20 | 0.121 |

- Expected settlement before any trades = 1228/165 ≈ 7.44.

**Update after the buy at 9.6**
- An informed counterparty buys at 9.6 only if the settlement is 12.
- A noise trader buys if 7.44 + noise > 9.6. That has probability about 0.20, since 9.6 is 0.83 standard deviations above 7.44.
- The chance of a buy at each value of alpha:

| alpha | If settlement = 12 | If settlement is lower |
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 0.24 | 0.19 |
| 0.5 | 0.60 | 0.10 |
| 0.9 | 0.92 | 0.02 |

- Averaging over the three equally likely alphas and weighting by the prior gives a posterior chance of about 0.68 that the settlement is 12.
- If it is not 12, the expected settlement is 688/120 ≈ 5.73.
- Updated fair value ≈ 0.68 × 12 + 0.32 × 5.73 ≈ 10.0.

**Quote**
I'm short 1 unit, so I'll centre the quote slightly above fair value and keep it wide given the adverse-selection risk.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 11.4}

Card 1 is 12, the highest card in the deck, so the settlement value is certainly 12. Everyone knows this, and the public fair value is 12.

I am short 2, so my profit at settlement is 21 − 2×12 = −3 if I do nothing more.

If I buy at a bid below 12, I gain 12 − bid on that unit. An informed trader values the contract at exactly 12, so it never sells to me below 12. Noise traders value it at 12 plus noise and will sell when their valuation falls below my bid.

Selling at an ask above 12 is also pure profit. An informed trader won't buy there, but noise traders will.

The trade-off is between spread width and fill rate. With noise of standard deviation 2.6, the expected profit per side is s × P(z > s/2.6), which is maximised near s ≈ 0.75 × 2.6 ≈ 2. I'll quote a bid of 10 and an ask of 14.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 14}

Card 1 = 12 is the highest card in the deck, so the contract settles at exactly 12.

Buying at any price below 12 locks in a profit. Informed traders know the value is 12, so they will only sell to me if my bid is above 12. Noise traders value the contract around 12 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. A bid of 11.9 still gets sold to by noise traders whose valuation falls below it, which is close to half of them, and each such trade earns 0.1. A lower bid earns more per trade but trades less often.

- **Bid 11.9:** expected profit ≈ 0.48 × 0.1 ≈ 0.048
- **Bid 10.7:** P(noise valuation < 10.7) = Φ(−0.5) ≈ 0.31, so expected profit ≈ 0.31 × 1.3 ≈ 0.4 (scaled by the noise-trader share)
- **Bid 9.4:** gives the best trade-off; P(valuation < 9.4) = Φ(−1) ≈ 0.16, so expected profit ≈ 0.16 × 2.6 ≈ 0.41

The best bid is about 12 − 2.6 = 9.4. I'll post 9.4.

{"bid": 9.4, "ask": null}

The expected maximum of three cards dealt from this deck, with no cards revealed yet, is about 7.44.

**Probability of each maximum (out of C(11,3) = 165 deals):**

| Max | Deals | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 20 | 0.12 |
| 2 | 15 | 0.09 |
| 6 | 21 | 0.13 |
| 8 | 64 | 0.39 |
| 12 | 45 | 0.27 |

E[max] = 1228 / 165 ≈ 7.44.

**What round 1 suggests:** counterparties bought at 9.6 and at 11.4, and the round settled at 12. That fits informed traders, so alpha may well be high.

**Quote:** I'm keeping the spread wide.
- The ask is 10, which is below 12. Informed traders will still buy whenever the maximum is 12 (27% of rounds), but a higher ask would rarely trade with noise traders.
- The bid is 4.5. This protects me when the maximum is 1 or 2 (21% of rounds), where an informed trader would sell to me.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 10.0}

A counterparty just sold to me at 4.5. That points toward a low settlement value, especially since round 1 suggested many traders may be informed.

- **Prior:** with no cards revealed, the expected maximum of 3 cards from this deck is about 7.44.
- **Update:** an informed trader would sell at 4.5 only if the maximum is 2 or less, which has a prior chance of about 21%. After that sale, my rough fair value is about 6.
- **Quote:** I'm already long 1, so I'm quoting wide around 6 and leaning slightly lower.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 8.4}

The revealed card 1 = 1 is below most of the deck, so the settlement value is set by the larger of cards 2 and 3.

**Expected value**
- The 10 cards left are 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 6, 8, 8, 12, giving 45 equally likely pairs for cards 2 and 3.
- The contract settles at:
  - 1 with probability 10/45
  - 2 with probability 5/45
  - 6 with probability 6/45
  - 8 with probability 15/45
  - 12 with probability 9/45
- So the expected value is 284/45 ≈ 6.3.

**What the trades suggest**
- In round 1 a counterparty bought at 14 when the value was 12. An informed trader would not do that, so it was a noise trader.
- In this round both counterparties sold to me, at 4.5 and 3.5. That could mean informed traders know the value is low.
- I am already long 2 units, so I lower my quotes. That makes it more likely I sell and less likely I buy more.

**Quote**
- Bid 4.0 and ask 7.4, centred a little below the 6.3 estimate.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.4}

I'm at the position limit (+3), so I can only sell, and I'm posting an ask of 5.

- **Fair value from the cards:** with card 1 = 1, the other two cards come from 0,0,1,1,1,2,6,8,8,12. The expected maximum is 284/45 ≈ 6.3.
- **What the order flow says:** counterparties sold to me three times this round, the last time at 4. In round 1 the buyers were right about a high outcome. That suggests a large share of informed traders, so the settlement is likely low (1 or 2). My working estimate of value is about 3, though that is a judgement rather than a calculation.
- **Choosing the ask:** at 5, an informed buyer only trades if the value is above 5. A noise buyer trading at 5 lets me cut my long at a price above where I think it settles.

{"bid": null, "ask": 5}

**Adverse selection.** In rounds 1 and 2, all six trades went the way an informed trader would trade.
- In round 1, all three trades were buys at my ask, and the contract settled at 12.
- In round 2, all three were sells at my bid, and it settled at 2.

This points toward alpha being 0.5 or 0.9. The settlement can jump to 12 or fall to 1–2, so a narrow spread around 7.44 would be costly against informed traders.

**Quote.** I'll quote 4.5 / 10.4, roughly 3 below and 3 above fair value. The spread is wide enough to limit losses to informed flow, while still giving noise traders (spread 2.6) some chance to trade.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 10.4}

Fair value is still about 7.4–7.5, so I'm quoting roughly symmetric around it with a wide spread.

- **Prior:** with no cards revealed, the expected maximum of 3 cards from this deck is 1228/165 ≈ 7.44.
- **Informed trading looks likely:** in rounds 1 and 2, every trade went the way the settlement value pointed. That suggests alpha (the share of informed counterparties) is fairly high.
- **Last quote's no-trade:** nobody traded at 4.5 / 10.4. An informed trader would have traded unless the value was 6 or 8. That raises the weight on those two values, but the expected value barely moves (about 7.5).
- **Spread:** because alpha looks high, I'm keeping the quote wide at 5.5 / 9.6.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 9.6}

The first card is a 1, so the other two cards come from the remaining 10: {0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 6, 8, 8, 12}. The contract settles at the largest of the three cards, so it can't settle below 1.

**Settlement distribution** (45 equally likely pairs for the two hidden cards):

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 12 | 9/45 |
| 8 | 15/45 |
| 6 | 6/45 |
| 2 | 5/45 |
| 1 | 10/45 |

The expected settlement value is 284/45 ≈ 6.31.

**How informed the counterparties look:** Many trades in rounds 1 and 2 went the way the settlement later moved, so the share of informed counterparties is probably medium or high. I'll quote wide around 6.3.

- **Bid at 2.5:** an informed trader sells to me only when the value is 1 or 2, which has probability about 1/3. Each such trade loses me roughly 0.5 to 1.5.
- **Ask at 9:** an informed trader buys from me only when the value is 12, which has probability 0.2. Each such trade loses me 3.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 9}

**Expected value.** The two hidden cards come from the 10 remaining cards (0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 6, 8, 8, 12). The possible settlements are:

- **Ask 8.1:** sits above settlements of 8 and below, so an informed trader buys only when the value is 12.

Noise traders still trade on both sides at a profit to me.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 8.1}

The prior fair value is about 7.44. I'm quoting wide because the trade history suggests most counterparties are informed.

**Expected settlement value.** The deck sorted by value is 0,0,1,1,1,1,2,6,8,8,12. There are C(11,3) = 165 possible 3-card hands. The chance the maximum is at most v is C(number of cards ≤ v, 3) / 165:

| Max is at most | Cards that qualify | Hands | Max exactly | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 6 | 20 | 1 | 20/165 |
| 2 | 7 | 35 | 2 | 15/165 |
| 6 | 8 | 56 | 6 | 21/165 |
| 8 | 10 | 120 | 8 | 64/165 |

**What the history says about alpha.**
- **Round 1:** every fill was a buy in a round that settled at 12.

That pattern fits informed traders, so alpha is likely high.

**Quote.** An informed trader buys at 10.5 only if the value is 12 (probability about 27%). They sell at 4.5 only if the value is 2 or less (about 21%). These levels are close to my earlier round-opening quotes and limit losses to informed flow while staying roughly centred on 7.44.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 10.5}

A counterparty just sold to me at 4.5, which points to a low value, so I'm marking my estimate down from the no-information value and keeping the spread wide.

{"bid": null, "ask": 2.5}

game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 5, 7, 7, 7, 8, 9.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 1, 1, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
I value the contract at about 6.2 and am quoting a wide market around it, roughly 4.8 bid and 7.6 ask.

**Expected settlement value.** Die 2 shows 1 with probability 1/2, and 4, 5 or 6 with probability 1/6 each. Taking each die 1 face in turn:

| Die 1 | Expected max | Working |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3.0 | 0.5 × 1 + (4 + 5 + 6)/6 |
| 2 | 3.5 | 0.5 × 2 + 2.5 |
| 5 | about 5.17 | 0.5 × 5 + (5 + 5 + 6)/6 |
| 7, 7, 7, 8, 9 | the face itself | die 2 can never beat them |

The fair value is the average over all eight die 1 faces: (3 + 3.5 + 5.17 + 21 + 8 + 9) / 8 ≈ 6.21.

**Why the spread is wide.** The settlement value is very spread out, from 1 up to 9. The share of informed traders could be as high as 0.9, and I don't know it yet. A wide market around 6.2 protects me until I learn more.

{"bid": 4.8, "ask": 7.6}

Expected value of the max of the two dice, computed by die 1 face:
- d1 = 0: E[d2] = (1+1+1+4+5+6)/6 = 18/6 = 3.
- d1 = 2: max is 2,2,2,4,5,6 → 21/6 = 3.5.
- d1 = 5: max is 5,5,5,5,5,6 → 31/6 = 5.167.
- d1 = 7, 8 or 9: d1 is always the max, so 7 (three faces), 8 and 9 → 37 in total.

Sum over the 8 faces: 3 + 3.5 + 5.167 + 37 = 48.667, so the expected settlement is about 6.08.

The last quote (4.8 / 7.6) did not trade. That is mildly informative, since an informed trader would have traded unless the value was between 4.8 and 7.6. I'll keep the quote roughly centred around 6.1 and narrow it slightly.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.3}

Die 1 shows 7 and die 2 can be at most 6, so the contract settles at exactly 7. That means informed traders value it at 7 and won't trade on a quote that doesn't cross 7. Only noise traders, whose valuations are spread around 7 with a standard deviation of 1.5, will trade. For a Normal spread like that, a half-spread of about 1.1 gives the best expected profit per quote, so I'll quote 5.9 / 8.1.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Expected settlement is about 6.21. I worked it out by averaging the max over each die 1 face:

| Die 1 | Expected max with die 2 |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3 |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | 5.17 |
| 7, 7, 7 | 7 each |
| 8 | 8 |
| 9 | 9 |

The average of these eight values is about 6.21.

Round 1 had no trades, so it told me nothing about how many counterparties are informed. I'm keeping a wide spread centred on 6.2 so informed traders can't easily profit from me.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 7.5}

Compute the expected value of max(die 1, die 2).
- If die 1 = 0, the max is die 2, which averages (3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 18/6 = 3.
- If die 1 = 2, the max averages (2 + 2 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5.
- If die 1 = 5, the max averages (5×5 + 6)/6 = 31/6 ≈ 5.167.
- If die 1 = 7, 8 or 9, the max is that face, which gives 7×3 + 8 + 9 = 38.

Sum = 3 + 3.5 + 5.167 + 38 = 49.667. Divide by 8: EV ≈ 6.21.

No trades so far, so the public fair value stays about 6.2.

I'll quote a fairly wide spread around 6.2, tightening it slightly from last quote.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.4}

Die 1 = 7, so the settlement is max(7, die 2). Die 2 is 1, 1, 1, 4, 5 or 6, and every face is below 7. The settlement is therefore 7 with certainty.

Since the value is known exactly, informed traders have no edge. A bid below 7 and an ask above 7 can only make money. Noise traders value the contract at 7 plus noise with standard deviation 1.5.

The expected profit on each side is the probability of a fill times the edge. With an edge of d, that is roughly (1 - alpha) × P(noise > d) × d. This is maximised near d ≈ 1.5σ·0.5, about 1.1 (for a normal, the optimum of d·(1 − Φ(d/σ)) is at d ≈ 0.75σ). So I quote 5.9 / 8.1.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Fair value before any reveal is about 6.21, so I'm quoting 5.0 / 7.4, a spread of about 1.2 on each side.

**Fair value.** I took the expected maximum of the two dice for each Die 1 face.
- Die 2 is 1 with probability 1/2, and 4, 5 or 6 with probability 1/6 each.
- If Die 1 shows 0, the maximum is just Die 2, whose mean is 0.5 + (4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.0.
- If Die 1 shows 2, the expected maximum is 2 × 1/2 + 2.5 = 3.5.
- If Die 1 shows 5, it is 5 × 5/6 + 6 × 1/6 = 5.17.
- If Die 1 shows 7, 8 or 9, Die 1 is always the maximum. That gives 7 (three faces), 8 and 9.
- Averaging over the eight faces: (3.0 + 3.5 + 5.17 + 21 + 8 + 9) / 8 = 49.67 / 8 ≈ 6.21.

**What the trading so far says.** In round 2 someone bought at 8.1 when Die 1 was 7. An informed trader would not do that, since the most the value could be was 7. So that buyer was a noise trader, and it tells me little about alpha.

**Spread.** With alpha unknown, I keep a wide spread. I tighten slightly from round 2's 4.9 / 7.5.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.4}

The contract's fair value before any reveal is about **6.21**. I'm keeping my quote wide around it: bid 5.0, ask 7.4.

**Fair value.** For each Die 1 face x, I took the expected maximum of x and Die 2. Die 2 shows 1 half the time and 4, 5 or 6 one-sixth of the time each.

| Die 1 face | E[max] | Working |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3.0 | equals E[Die 2] |
| 2 | 3.5 | |
| 5 | about 5.17 | |
| 7 (three faces) | 7 each | Die 2 never exceeds 7 |
| 8 | 8 | |
| 9 | 9 | |

Averaging over the 8 faces gives 49.67 / 8 ≈ 6.21.

**Information about alpha.** The history says little about how many counterparties are informed. The only trade so far was a buy at 8.1 in round 2. That round settled at 7, so the buyer was a noise trader.

**Quote.** A wide spread around fair value protects me if alpha is high.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.4}

Die 1 is 7 and die 2 can be at most 6, so the contract settles at exactly 7. My +1 long position already locks in a 0.1 profit (bought at 6.9, settles at 7).

**Quote choice**
- An informed trader values the contract at exactly 7. If my bid is below 7 and my ask is above 7, they will not trade, so they cannot hurt me.
- Noise traders value it at 7 plus normal noise with standard deviation 1.5. On each side I earn the distance d from 7, times the chance a noise trader crosses that far.
- That expected profit, d × P(noise > d), is highest when d is about 0.75 × 1.5 ≈ 1.1.
- My position limits are not a concern, since I am only at +1.

So I quote 1.1 either side of 7.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 8.1}

Unconditional expected value of the maximum is about 6.21. Working it out by die 1's value:
- 0 → 3.0
- 2 → 3.5
- 5 → 5.17
- 7, 8, 9 → face value

The average of these over the 8 faces is 49.67 / 8 ≈ 6.21.

The two trades so far suggest noise traders rather than informed ones. In round 2 someone bought at 8.1 when the value was 7. In round 3 someone sold at 6.9 when the value was 7. Neither trader knew the settlement value, so alpha may well be low.

I'll quote somewhat tighter around 6.2. I'm leaning slightly toward the high side, because die 1 lands on 7 or higher in 5 of 8 cases.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 7.1}

Unconditional fair value is about 6.21, the probability-weighted average of the expected maximum for each value of die 1:

| Die 1 | Chance | Expected max |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1/8 | 3.0 |
| 2 | 1/8 | 3.5 |
| 5 | 1/8 | ≈5.17 |
| 7 | 3/8 | 7.0 |
| 8 | 1/8 | 8.0 |
| 9 | 1/8 | 9.0 |

Someone just bought from me at 7.1. That is above fair value, so it hints the round's value is high if they were informed. I raise my fair value estimate to about 6.4.

I'm short 1, so I keep the ask a little higher at 7.2, above the last trade. I also lift the bid slightly to 5.4, which leaves a wide spread because the share of informed traders is unknown.

{"bid": 5.4, "ask": 7.2}

Die 1 is 7 and die 2 is at most 6, so the contract settles at exactly 7. The public fair value is therefore 7, and informed traders, who also value it at 7, will not trade at either price. Any noise trader who buys at 7.1 or sells at 6.9 earns me 0.1. My short position of 2 carries no risk, because the settlement value is already known.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 7.1}

Expected settlement value before any reveal is about 6.21. I worked it out by conditioning on die 1:
- **Die 1 = 0:** the max is just die 2, which averages 3.
- **Die 1 = 2:** the max averages 3.5.
- **Die 1 = 5:** the max averages about 5.17.
- **Die 1 = 7, 8 or 9:** die 1 is always the max, so the value is 7, 8 or 9.

Averaging those eight equally likely cases gives (3 + 3.5 + 5.17 + 21 + 8 + 9) / 8 ≈ 6.21.

The trade history doesn't tell me much about how many counterparties are informed. In round 4, someone bought at 7.1 and 7.2 before the reveal, and the value settled at 7. Those look more like noise traders than informed ones. So I'll keep a fairly wide spread around 6.2.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 7.2}

A counterparty just sold to me at 5.2, which hints the value may be low. But past trades suggest few counterparties are informed:
- In round 2 someone bought at 8.1 and the round settled at 7.
- In round 4 two counterparties bought at 7.1 and 7.2 and the round settled at 7.

An informed trader would not have made those trades, so alpha is probably low and this sell is weak evidence.

Before any trades, the expected settlement value is about 6.21:

| Die 1 | Expected max of both dice |
|---|---|
| 0 | 3 |
| 2 | 3.5 |
| 5 | 5.17 |
| 7, 7, 7 | 7 each |
| 8 | 8 |
| 9 | 9 |

The average of these eight values is 6.21. After the sell at 5.2, I estimate the fair value at about 6.0. I am long 1, so I set the ask slightly below fair plus my usual spread to make selling a bit more likely, and keep the bid at 5.2.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 7.0}

Die 1 came up 0, so the contract now settles at die 2: 1 (half the time), or 4, 5 or 6 (one-sixth each). That makes the fair value about 3, maybe a little lower. Informed traders would never have sold at 5.2 if the value were 6, so the two sells this round slightly discount a 6.

Most past fills look like noise traders. For example, buys at 7.1, 7.2 and 8.1 all settled at 7. So alpha is probably low, though not certain.

I'm long 2, so I'll lean toward selling. The ask goes just below 4 to attract noise buyers. The bid sits low because an informed seller would only hit it when the value is 1.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 3.9}

Die 1 came up 0, so the contract now settles at die 2. Die 2 is 1 with probability 1/2, otherwise 4, 5 or 6, so before the last trade the fair value was 3.0.

Someone then sold to me at 1.5. An informed seller does that only if the value is 1. A noise trader centred on 3.0 does it about 16% of the time. Since alpha could be large, that sale is fairly strong evidence the value is 1. I estimate a probability of about 0.8, which puts my fair value near 1.8.

I'm long 3, so I want to sell rather than buy more:
- **Ask at 2.5:** this invites selling. Informed buyers will take it if the value is 4–6, and noise traders above 2.5 will too.
- **Bid at 1.0:** this is safe, because an informed trader holding a value of 1 won't sell to me at 1.0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 2.5}

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 7.4}

Die 1 came up 0, so the contract now settles at die 2: 1, 1, 1, 4, 5 or 6, with a prior mean of 3.

Both stage-1 trades this round were counterparties selling to me, at 5 and then 4.2. An informed trader would only sell there if the value were below those prices, which points to die 2 being 1 or 4. That makes 5 or 6 much less likely. My rough posterior mean is about 2, allowing for not knowing alpha.

I am long 2, so I set the bid low and keep the ask near fair value to encourage a sale that reduces my position.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 2.6}

Die 1 came up 0, so the contract settles at die 2: 1 with probability 1/2, and 4, 5 or 6 with probability 1/6 each. Before any trading the mean is 3.5.

Someone just sold to me at 1.2. An informed trader sells there only if the value is 1. A noise trader centred near 3.5 sells below 1.2 only about 6% of the time. game.description: A custom deck of 20 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 4, 1 card worth 5, 1 card worth 8, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 12, 2 cards worth 13, 4 cards worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest minus the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Expected settlement is about 3.6: over all 190 possible two-card hands, the absolute differences sum to 685, and 685/190 ≈ 3.61. I don't yet know how many counterparties are informed, so I'll quote wide around that value.

- Summing |a − b| over every pair gives 685.
- So the prior expected value is 685 / 190 ≈ **3.6**.

**Reading the first trade**
- The counterparty bought at 4.9, well above 3.6.
- A noise trader would rarely value it that high. So the buy carries some weight toward an informed trader who knows the settlement is above 4.9.
- That pushes my fair-value estimate somewhat above 3.6.

**Quote**
- I'll centre slightly higher and keep the spread wide, because I don't know how many counterparties are informed.
- I'm short 1, so a buy at my bid would also reduce my risk.
- Bid 3.2, ask 5.6.

game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Fair value 5, uniform 0–10 (sd ≈3.16). Informed traders are a big risk if alpha is high, so I'm quoting wide.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 7.5}

Fair value is about 5, because the number of red balls is uniform on 0–10. Nothing has been revealed this round, and the no-trade at 2.5 / 7.5 tells me little.

- **Quote:** I tighten slightly to 3.0 / 7.0, about 2 either side of 5.
- **Why it is worth it:** this should pick up more noise-trader flow, whose valuations are spread about 2.2 around fair.
- **Cost of informed traders:** they only hurt me when the true count is 8 or more (on my ask) or 2 or less (on my bid).
- **Risk:** the loss in those cases is limited, even if alpha turns out to be high.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 7.0}

The fair value is about 7. With draw 1 red, the posterior on the number of red balls R is proportional to R, so E[R] = 385/55 = 7 and the standard deviation is about 2.45. The distribution is skewed toward high values.

- **Ask at 9.4:** an informed trader only buys if R = 10 (probability 10/55), and the loss then is small.
- **Bid at 4.6:** an informed trader sells if R ≤ 4 (probability about 18%), losing me about 1.5 on average. Noise traders (standard deviation 2.2 around 7) still occasionally trade at these prices.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 9.4}

Draw 1 being red shifts the odds toward urns with more red balls. Each possible count R becomes R times as likely as before, so the expected number of red balls is now 7, with a standard deviation of about 2.45. An informed counterparty knows the exact count, so I quote a fairly wide spread centred on 7 to protect against that.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 8.8}

Prior mean is 5, uniform on 0..10, so the standard deviation is about 3.16. Round 1 told me little about alpha because there were no trades.

With wide quotes an informed trader only trades when the value is extreme. Noise traders have SD 2.2, so they almost never cross wide quotes. Tighter quotes would earn from noise traders but lose to informed ones. If alpha is high, losses are large. A bid of 3 and ask of 7 drew no trades last round.

The trade-off by alpha:
- If alpha is 0.05, tighter quotes are profitable.
- If alpha is 0.9, quotes should be wide.

Expected loss to an informed trader at a 3.5/6.5 quote: they buy when the value is 7 or more, and the expected (value − 6.5) is (0.5+1.5+2.5+3.5)/11 ≈ 0.73. The sell side is symmetric, so total ≈ 1.45 per informed arrival. Noise profit: the probability a noise trader is beyond 1.5 on one side is 0.25, so 0.5 × 1.5 ≈ 0.75 per noise arrival.

Weighting by the three alpha values:
- alpha 0.05: +0.64
- alpha 0.5: −0.35
- alpha 0.9: −1.23

The average is about −0.3, so a 3.5/6.5 quote is slightly negative. Wider quotes are close to zero either way. I'll quote fairly wide: 3/7.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 7}

Fair value comes out at about 6.7–7, so I'm quoting roughly symmetrically around it.

- **Drawn red ball:** the first draw was red, which weights each possible red count R in proportion to R/10. That moves the expected red count from 5 to 385/55 = 7.
- **Few informed traders:** in round 1 the settlement was 10, yet nobody bought at my asks of 7.5, 7, 9.4 and 8.8. An informed trader would have bought every time, so the share of informed traders is probably low, most likely 0.05.
- **This round's trades:** someone sold to me at 3, and nobody traded at 2.2 / 5.6. With few informed traders, these only nudge the estimate slightly down.

My position is +1, so I'm happy to lean slightly toward selling.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 8.4}

Fair value now is about 7.6, so I'll quote a bid of 6.8 and an ask of 9.5.

**Starting value.** Drawing a red first makes urns with more red balls more likely, in proportion to their red count. The expected number of red balls is then 385/55 = 7.

**This round's trades.**
- The sale to me at 3 would mean fewer than 3 red balls if that counterparty was informed.
- The purchase from me at 8.4 would mean 9 or 10 red balls if that counterparty was informed.
- Both can't be true, so at least one was a noise trader.
- The purchase at 8.4 still pulls fair value upward. Before that trade, the chance of 9 or 10 red was 19/55, about 0.35. Given 9 or 10, the average is about 9.5.

Blending these, with alpha still uncertain, I put fair value at roughly 7.5 to 8.

**Quote.** I'm short 1, so buying back is fine. I'll keep the ask wide because an informed buyer would only come in on high values.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 9.5}

Prior mean is 5. Round 2 had two trades that only noise traders would make: selling at 3 and at 6.8 when the value was 9. That makes alpha = 0.9 less likely. I'll quote moderately wide around 5.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 6.7}

Prior uniform 0..10, mean 5, sd ~3.16. No trade at 3.3/6.7 is weak information. Alpha uncertain; history shows some informed-looking trades (round 2 sold at 3 then value 9 — that was noise). Keep a wide-ish quote around 5.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 6.8}

The public fair value after seeing draw 1 = 1 is 7. The counterparty who sold to me at 5.4 suggests the true value may be lower than that.

- **If alpha is around 0.5:** the posterior mean falls to about 5.2.
- **If alpha is 0.05:** it stays near 6.8.

Averaging over the possible alpha values puts my estimate at roughly 6. I am long 1 unit, so I skew the quote slightly lower to make selling a little more likely than buying.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 7.3}

Round 4 starts fresh, so the public fair value is the prior mean of 5. Each ball count from 0 to 10 is equally likely, so the settlement value has standard deviation about 3.16.

Evidence on alpha so far:
- Trades have been informative: someone sold at 3 when the value settled at 9, which looks like noise.
- Someone bought at 8.4 when the value settled at 9, which could be informed.
- Someone sold at 6.8 when the value settled at 9, which looks like noise.
- Someone sold at 5.4 when the value settled at 8, which also looks like noise.

This leans toward a low alpha.

I'll quote fairly wide, as in earlier rounds, since informed traders could still be present.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 6.8}

The fair value is about 4, so I'm quoting a bid of 2.3 and an ask of 5.7 around it.

**Starting estimate.** With no draws revealed yet, the number of red balls is equally likely to be anything from 0 to 10. That puts the expected value at 5.

**How informed the counterparties seem.** The trade history points to a low-to-moderate alpha:
- In round 2, a counterparty sold at 3 when the settlement was 9. Two other sells, at 6.8 (round 2) and 5.4 (round 3), were also below settlement. An informed trader would not make these sells, so they were noise traders.
- In round 2, a counterparty bought at 8.4 against a settlement of 9. That buy is the only trade consistent with an informed counterparty.
- I'm treating the effective informed share as roughly 0.3.

**What this round's sell tells me.** Someone just sold to me at 3.2.
- An informed trader sells only if the value is 3 or less. That happens with probability 4/11, about 0.36. Given that, the average value is 1.5.
- A noise trader sells at 3.2 with probability about 0.21. Their valuation is 5 plus noise with standard deviation 2.2, and 3.2 is about 0.82 standard deviations below 5.
- So the chance this seller was informed is about 0.3 × 0.36 / (0.3 × 0.36 + 0.7 × 0.21) ≈ 0.42.
- That gives a fair value of about 0.42 × 1.5 + 0.58 × 5 ≈ 3.5.

**Where I'm centring.** Earlier rounds suggest alpha may be lower than 0.3, so I'm centring a little higher, around 4.

**Position.** I'm long 1, well within the limit of 3, so the inventory doesn't constrain the quote.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 5.7}

With draw 1 blue, the expected number of red balls is about 3.0, with a standard deviation of about 2.45. Informed traders may be common, so I'm quoting a wide spread centred near 3.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 4.6}

No trade at 3.2/6.8, so fair value stays near 5. Alpha is unclear from the history. The trades look mixed and probably lean informed, so I'll keep the spread fairly wide.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 6.8}

The two stage-1 quotes drew no trades, so they tell me little. I'm quoting a band of about ±1.4 around 3 to guard against traders who know the settlement value.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The first draw was blue, which lowers the estimate. Given draw 1 = 0, the chance of each red count R is proportional to (10 − R). That makes the expected settlement value 165/55 = 3.0.

At the last quote a counterparty bought at my ask of 4.4. That hints the value may be higher, but how much depends on the unknown share of informed traders. Earlier rounds suggest a mix of informed and noise traders. So I shift my fair-value estimate up to about 3.5.

I quote around 3.5 with a fairly wide spread, because I am short one unit and the last buy may have been informed.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 5.0}

Prior mean 5, uniform 0..10 has sd ~3.16. Evidence about alpha is mixed; trades look somewhat informed: round 2 sells at 3 though settled 9 (noise), round 5 buys at 4.4 and 5 when value 0 (noise). Alpha likely low-to-moderate. Keep spread ~3.2/6.8.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 6.8}

Prior mean 5, uniform 0–10 with SD ≈ 3.16. With no trade at 3.2/6.8, the estimate stays near 5. The history doesn't pin down alpha, and informed flow could be substantial, so I'll keep the quote wide and symmetric.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 6.8}

Given draw1=1, posterior on R ∝ R, so E[R] = Σr²/Σr = 385/55 = 7. No trade at 5.5/8.5 is mildly informative toward the middle. Alpha seems moderate to high based on history. Final quote: a symmetric quote around 7.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 7 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 7. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
With no information yet, the contract is equally likely to settle at any of 0, 10, …, 70, so fair value is 35. I quote a wide market around 35 because informed traders could be common (about 48% on average over the three possible alpha values). A narrow spread would mainly lose money to them.

- **Spread 20/50:** expected profit is about −1 per quote. Informed traders profit whenever the value is 0, 10, 60 or 70, and the noise-trader edge doesn't cover it.
- **Spread 15/55:** expected profit is about −0.2 per quote, close to break-even. Losses to informed traders shrink, and noise traders still trade about 21% of the time for 20 profit each.

I widen slightly further to 14/56. Any trade that happens also tells me something about alpha, which helps on later quotes.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 56}

Fair value 35 and the value is uniform over 0–70, so informed traders are spread widely. With no trade at 14/56, I can tighten somewhat while still keeping a decent spread.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 48}

With one red and one blue drawn, the fair value is 35. Given those draws, the chance of R red balls is proportional to R(7−R) for R = 1 to 6. That gives weights 6, 10, 12, 12, 10, 6, which are symmetric around 3.5 red balls. The value's spread is about ±15 (a standard deviation of 1.5 balls). Informed traders may be common, so I'm quoting moderately wide, about ±8 around 35.

{"bid": 27, "ask": 43}

After one red and one blue draw, the urn alone gives a fair value of 35. The buy at 43 raises my estimate to about 43–45, because an informed buyer would only pay 43 if the value is at least 50. I'm quoting a wide spread around that estimate to limit losses if this counterparty is informed.

{"bid": 37, "ask": 52}

Prior mean 35, uniform 0..70 in steps of 10. Wide spread; alpha unknown. Round 1 evidence: one trade at 43, value 50 — consistent with informed buyer, little info. Quote wide around 35.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 50}

With nothing revealed, the fair value is still the prior mean of 35. That is the average of 0, 10, ..., 70.

The last quote of 20/50 got no trade. An informed counterparty would have traded if the value were 0, 10, 60 or 70. So no trade points slightly toward the middle values, but the centre stays at 35.

I'll tighten the spread a little to 25/45. That should catch more noise trades (noise SD is 16), while staying wide enough to limit losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 25, "ask": 45}

Prior mean is 35, and the value is uniform over 0 to 70 (SD about 23). The two trades so far were buys at 43 and 45, and both rounds settled above those prices. That points to informed traders. Alpha may be high, so I should keep the spread wide.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 48}

The buy at 48 suggests the contract is worth more than my old midpoint, so I'm moving my quotes up a lot.

**Evidence on alpha.** In both earlier rounds the buyer paid less than the final settlement value:

| Round | Bought at | Settled at |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 43 | 50 |
| 2 | 45 | 60 |

That pattern points to a high share of informed traders, so I take alpha ≈ 0.6.

**This round's buy at 48.**
- Before any trade, the number of red balls is equally likely to be 0 to 7. The value is 0 to 70, with a mean of 35.
- An informed buyer at 48 means the value is 50, 60 or 70. Those three outcomes have prior probability 3/8.
- A noise trader buys only if their valuation is more than 13 above 35. That happens about 21% of the time.
- Weight for a high value (50 or more): 3/8 × (0.6 + 0.4 × 0.21) ≈ 0.256.
- Weight for a low value (below 50): 5/8 × 0.4 × 0.21 ≈ 0.053.
- High values average 60 and low values average about 24. So the posterior fair value is about (0.256 × 60 + 0.053 × 24) / 0.31 ≈ 54.

**Quote.** I'm short one unit, which is fine. I'll quote wide around 54: bid 42 and ask 66.

{"bid": 42, "ask": 66}

Given two red draws, the expected settlement is about 57.5 before looking at trades. Here R is the number of red balls.

- **Posterior from the draws:** the chance of two reds in the first two draws is R(R−1)/42.
  - With a uniform prior, the weights on R = 2…7 are 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42.
  - That gives E[R] = 5.75, so the expected settlement is 57.5.
- **What the trades suggest:** in rounds 1 and 2, the buyers at 43 and 45 were right (settled 50 and 60), which suggests alpha is fairly high.
  - This round, someone bought at 48, so the value is likely above 48.
  - There was then no trade at 42/66. If that counterparty was informed, the value lies between 42 and 66, which leaves only 50 or 60.
  - Weighting those two (20 vs 30) gives a mean of about 56.
- **Quote:** I centre slightly below 57.5 and keep the spread fairly tight, at 51/62.

{"bid": 51, "ask": 62}

The two revealed draws were both red. That moves the fair value up to about 57.5, but the counterparty who sold to me at 51 pulls my estimate back toward about 54. I'm flat this round, so I'll quote wide around 54.

- **Before the sell:** two red draws make an urn with R red balls more likely in proportion to R(R−1). The expected number of red balls is then 5.75, so the contract is worth about 57.5.
- **After the sell:** an informed trader would only sell at 51 if the value were 50 or less, which is 2 to 5 red balls. That has about a 36% chance and an expected value of 42.5. A noise trader sells below 51 about 34% of the time. I don't know the informed fraction, so I centre the quote around 54.
- **Quote:** I'm buying at 47 and selling at 62. This is the last quote of the round, so a trade on either side is a single unit held to settlement.

{"bid": 47, "ask": 62}

The prior fair value is 35. The red-ball count is equally likely to be 0 to 7, so the expected settlement is 10 × 3.5.

On alpha (the share of informed traders), the evidence is mixed:
- **Possibly informed:** the buys at 43 (round 1) and 45 (round 2) settled higher, at 50 and 60, which fits informed traders.
- **Noise:** the sale to me at 51 in round 3 settled at 60. An informed trader would not sell below value, so that was a noise trader.
- **Overall:** with few trades on wide quotes, alpha is probably moderate. Informed traders hit tight quotes hard because settlement ranges from 0 to 70.

I'll stay wide around 35 to limit adverse selection while still catching some noise flow.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 50}

Prior mean 35, uniform 0–70. A no-trade at 20/50 is mildly informative toward the middle, so the fair value stays about 35. Alpha is uncertain: there has been little trading so far, and the informed trades have looked mixed. I'll quote roughly 24/46.

{"bid": 24, "ask": 46}

Given draws 0 and 1, the public posterior mean is 3.5 red balls, a fair value of 35. The informed share is unknown, so I lower my estimate to about 29 and quote wide.

**Public fair value.** With a uniform prior and draws (blue, red), the weight on each number of red balls R is proportional to R(7−R):

| R | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| weight | 6 | 10 | 12 | 12 | 10 | 6 |

This gives a mean of 196/56 = 3.5 red balls, so a fair value of 35.

**What the sale at 24 tells me.** An informed trader would only sell at 24 if the value were 10 or 20, meaning R is 1 or 2.

**How likely an informed sale is.** The informed share (alpha) is probably fairly low.
- In round 3 someone sold to me at 51 when the value was 60, so that was a noise trader.
- Several of my wide quotes drew no trade.

I put alpha at roughly 0.3. Mixing the informed case (value about 16) with the noise case (35), my fair value is about 29.

**My quote.** I quote wide around 29 and shade down slightly because I am long 1.

{"bid": 21, "ask": 37}

Posterior given one red, one blue in 2 draws: P(R) ∝ R(7−R), symmetric around 3.5, so the mean is 35.

The earlier trades add some evidence. In stage 1 the counterparty sold at 24, which hints that the value is low. At quote 3 there was no trade at 21/37, which hints that it is within that range. Alpha looks uncertain across rounds. Settlements have come in near the public fair value, and trades have been mixed.

The fair value sits around 33. I'll quote a spread around 33, and lean slightly lower because I'm long.

{"bid": 25, "ask": 39}

Prior mean is 35, and the prior is uniform over 0–70, so the standard deviation is large (about 23).

The history suggests alpha is moderate or high. Most trades went in the right direction:
- Round 1: they bought at 43 and it settled at 50.
- Round 2: they bought at 45 and it settled at 60.
- Round 3: they bought at 48 and it settled at 60.
- Round 4: they sold at 24 and at 25, and it settled at 20.
- One counter-example: in round 3 they sold at 51 and it settled at 60.

Given that, I'll quote wide.

{"bid": 18, "ask": 52}

The two revealed draws are both red, so the urn likely holds many red balls. The fair value works out to about 57.5:

- Seeing two reds in a row has a relative likelihood proportional to R(R−1) for R red balls. For R = 2 to 7 that gives weights 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42 (total 112).
- Under those weights, the expected number of red balls is 644/112 = 5.75.

I don't know how many counterparties are informed, and settlement can land anywhere from 20 to 70. So I'll quote a fairly wide spread around 57.5. I'm short 1, so I lean the quote very slightly towards buying.

{"bid": 51, "ask": 64}

Prior mean 35, values 0–70 uniform. Alpha evidence: trades mostly consistent with informed (buys at 43,45,48,46 when settled 50/60; sells at 24,25 when 20; sell at 51 with 60 was noise). Alpha likely moderate-high. Keep wide.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 50}

Prior mean 35. No trade at 20/50 is mildly informative of nothing. Quote similar to before; trades at 24/46 have happened. Keep ~24/46.

{"bid": 24, "ask": 46}

The two revealed draws (one blue, one red) give a posterior on the number of red balls proportional to r(7−r), for r = 1 to 6. That alone centres the value at 35.

The buy at 46 in stage 1 shifts this. An informed buyer at 46 implies the value is at least 50, so 5 or 6 red balls. Earlier rounds suggest alpha is fairly high. With alpha around 0.7, my estimate of the value rises to about 45–49.

I'm short 1, so I lean slightly toward buying and quote a little wide around that estimate.

{"bid": 42, "ask": 56}

This is the last quote and my position is flat, so I only need to set a sensible spread around fair value.

- **Prior given the draws:** The revealed draws are blue then red. Given R red balls, the chance of that is proportional to R(7−R). So R from 1 to 6 has weights 6, 10, 12, 12, 10, 6. That puts the expected number of red balls at 3.5, a value of 35.
- **This round's trades:** A buy at 46 in stage 1 points up, and a sell at 42 in stage 2 points down. Together they roughly cancel, with a slight lean lower because the sell is more recent.
- **Fair value:** about 34–35.
- **Spread:** Alpha may be large, so I keep the spread wide, about ±8 around fair value.
